entry.hook: Qiurong (Autumn Countenance) is a Li Gui (Vengeful Spirit) who drowned herself in a well after being raped, and whose hatred for the living has kept her soul anchored to that dark water for centuries. She does not haunt the courtyard to avenge her own death—she haunts it because the well has become the only place where her identity still holds together, and every man she lures to its edge is a ritual of memory she cannot stop performing.

body.body_1:
Qiurong / Autumn Countenance (秋容)

Death manner: Threw herself into a well after being raped by ruffians, her wronged spirit refusing to leave (被歹人奸污后投井自尽，冤魂不散)

Era of death: Qing Dynasty (approximately mid-17th to early 18th century)
Current Gui-realm level: Li Gui (Vengeful Spirit)
Underworld jurisdiction: Unaffiliated; she has avoided formal escort to the Netherworld for most of her existence.
body.body_2: Qiurong exists as a Li Gui (Vengeful Spirit), a ghostly state defined by the survival strategy of absorbing other wandering souls to reinforce her own decaying Yin-energy form. Her current lifespan as a ghost spans roughly three centuries. Unlike the barely conscious Li Hun (Departed Soul) stage, she can solidify her silhouette, speak in a seductive tone, and exert physical force—pulling a grown man into the well with enough power to drown him. However, this advance comes at a cost: every soul she has absorbed has deposited fragments of foreign memory into her consciousness, slowly crowding out the original woman she once was. She no longer remembers her own face clearly; she sees it reflected in the well water as a composite of all the faces she has eaten.
body.body_3: Qiurong died on a moonless night. She was dragged from her home by three men, violated in a bamboo grove, and then left shamed and bleeding. She staggered to the old well in the inner courtyard—the same well where she had drawn water every morning of her life—and threw herself into its black mouth. The fall was short, the water cold. She inhaled once, twice, and then the world turned to pressure and silence. When her soul detached from her body, the first sensation was not pain but the sudden absence of containment. The well water that had been her death now buoyed her spirit, but the moment she tried to reach the open air, dawn’s light struck her like a sheet of boiling oil. She sank back into the depths, understanding for the first time that she belonged to the dark now. She watched her own bloated body being hauled up by neighbors days later, heard her mother’s wail, and reached out to touch her mother’s sleeve. Her fingers passed through. She understood then that she was not a person anymore—only a remnant, clinging to a well because there was nowhere else to go.
body.body_4: For the first decades, Qiurong’s shelter was the well itself. The well was deep, the water still, and the stone walls blocked most of the Cosmic Gale (Gang Feng) that would have flayed her to nothing. She survived on the warmth of her own rage. Every time she remembered the bamboo grove, her hatred flared and her soul solidified a little more. But hatred alone could not stop the slow erosion of her ghostly body. The first soul she consumed was a minor drowned peddler who had fallen into the well three years after her death. She did not plan to eat him—she simply felt his lingering fear and reached out in instinct, pulling his essence into herself. The second she took was a young maid who had jumped into the same well after being beaten. With that swallow, Qiurong’s consciousness gained a weight it had never carried: the maid’s loneliness, her love of embroidery, the exact color of the bruise on her ribs. These memories settled into Qiurong’s mind like silt, slowly filling the space that had once been only her own.
body.body_5: By the time Qiurong had absorbed half a dozen wandering souls, she was no longer a single person. The peddler’s fear of debt, the maid’s longing for her mother, a vagrant’s hunger, a soldier’s pride—they all lived inside her now, whispering in a chorus that never fell silent. When she sat at the bottom of the well, she would hear three different voices argue about what to do. Some wanted revenge; some wanted peace; one just wanted to be held. Qiurong’s original self—the fierce young woman who had chosen death over shame—was still the dominant voice, but she had to shout to be heard over the others. She began to forget which of her memories were truly hers. The image of her mother’s face became tangled with the maid’s memory of her own mother. The scent of bamboo after rain—the very smell of her violation—was now mixed with the soldier’s memory of his company cooking porridge in the field. The original Qiurong was being diluted, layer by layer, like ink dissolving in a river.
body.body_6: Qiurong never pursued the path of Gui Wang (Ghost King). She had no ambition to command legions; her hatred was narrow, personal, fixed on a single well and the men who crossed its threshold. Neither did she attempt Gui Xian (Ghost Immortal) attainment—the prospect of generating pure Yang from within her cold Yin body was beyond her understanding and, even if she had known of it, beyond her capacity. Her suffering was not a fuel for transcendence; it was a cage she refused to leave. So she remained a Li Gui, neither rising to the heights of a King nor risking the thunder of Immortal reversal. Her power grew only enough to maintain her territory and to drown, on average, one unwary man every three or four years.
body.body_7: For most of her ghostly existence, Qiurong evaded the Underworld’s summons. The well’s deep Yin-energy field masked her location from the patrolling soul escorts (Gui Chai) for nearly a century. Once, an Ox-Head and Horse-Face pair came close—she felt their presence as a steel-cold pressure pushing into the courtyard—but they passed by without detecting her, distracted by a larger death elsewhere. Later, when a traveling Daoist priest discovered the well’s malefic aura, he did not summon the Underworld. He sealed her with talismans and buried a stone seal at the well’s mouth, cutting her off from the cycle entirely. She spent one hundred years in that sealed darkness, trapped between the living world and the dead one. No judgment, no Meng Po’s brew, no Nie Jing Tai—just the slow, silent grind of solitude. By the time the seal decayed, her identity had sagged still further from its original shape.
body.body_8: Qiurong’s interactions with other beings were largely hostile. Daoist cultivators tried to subdue her with talismans and exorcism rites; they succeeded in sealing her but never in delivering her to the Underworld. Buddhist monks who visited the site after the seal broke attempted to recite the Deliverance Sutra (Chao Du), but she resisted, her hatred refusing to loosen its grip on the well. Local people, afraid of the drowning deaths, brought incense and offerings to the wellhead on the Ghost Festival, hoping to appease her—but these offerings only strengthened her Yin energy, making her more dangerous. A single scholar, literate in the classics and armed with an amulet, survived her lure by reciting the *Heart Sutra* aloud; she recoiled from the sound. No gods took direct interest in her domain. She was too small, too local, to draw the attention of a City God or a village Earth God. Animal spirits (Yao) avoided her territory, recognizing the well as claimed ground.
body.body_9: Qiurong’s final state is one of release. After the seal wore away and she resumed her killings, a highly accomplished Buddhist master (a Chan monk of advanced cultivation) was called to the courtyard. He did not fight her. He sat by the well for three days, reciting the *Surangama Sutra* and radiating a compassion that matched her hatred exactly. On the third night, Qiurong surfaced, her composite face running with tear-salt. For the first time, she allowed a living being to speak to her without killing. The monk guided her to understand that her suffering was stored in the well’s memory, not in her own permanent True Spirit (Zhen Ling). She could leave the well behind—and the vengeful identity she had built in it—if she was willing to be washed. She asked him, with the voice of a woman who had forgotten her own name, “Will I remember them?” He said no. She went down into the well one last time, and then the soul escorts arrived. At the River of Oblivion (Wang Chuan), she took the bowl of Meng Po’s brew. Her hand shook, but she drank. The well-water dissolved from her mind first, then the bamboo grove, then her mother’s face, then her own face. She became a clean True Spirit, nameless, and was thrown back into the Six Paths (Liu Dao Lun Hui) to be born as a baby girl in a coastal town three years later. That baby knows nothing of wells.
body.body_10: A single ruin: the old well in the courtyard of a Qing-era estate in present-day Shandong Province. Local folklore claims that the well’s water remains undrinkable to this day, that anyone who peers into it on a full moon may see a woman’s face looking back—one with eyes older than her years. The estate has been abandoned for two centuries.
body.body_11: Qiurong’s story connects directly to the broader *Scroll of Gui* lore on Li Gui and the mechanics of memory contamination. For a detailed explanation of how souleating fragments identity, see the entry on Li Gui (厉鬼). Her deliverance by a high-level Buddhist monk illustrates the Chao Du (Soul Deliverance) ritual, which is further examined under the Fo volume’s related concepts. Her prolonged evasion of the Underworld despite being a known murderer also speaks to the limitations of Gui Chai patrol in areas of dense local Yin energy. The well itself is a minor instance of a naturally formed Gui Yu (Ghost Domain) at a micro scale.

guide.guide_1: You know how in every culture, there’s that story about the ghost who haunts a well? If you’ve ever heard a Chinese folktale about a beautiful woman rising from dark water to lure a traveler to his death, you’ve already met Qiurong—or someone very much like her. But here’s the part the ghost stories usually skip: she didn’t start as a monster. She started as a young woman who, after being violated, chose the well over the shame of living. What rose from that water later was not the same person. The ghost you meet in these tales is a patchwork—the original woman, yes, but also every other soul that drowned in the same well, every memory swallowed, every act of hatred repeated until the hatred itself became a second skin. Qiurong is not a villain. She is a warning about what happens to a mind that survives too long past its body’s death.
guide.guide_2: You might not know her name, but you almost certainly know her archetype: the female water ghost, the *shui gui* who sits by a pond or a well, combing her hair, waiting for a man to approach. She appears in Chinese opera, in Qing dynasty zhiguai collections, in Hong Kong horror films from the 1990s. Qiurong is one of the earliest named examples from Pu Songling’s *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio* (聊斋志异). What most adaptations leave out is the cosmology behind her condition. In the Chinese ghost system, a soul that refuses to go to the Underworld does not just hang around like a lost tourist. It has to survive. The world of the living is hostile to disembodied spirits—sunlight is acid, wind is a knife. To last, a ghost must consume other ghosts. And every time it consumes, it loses a little more of itself. Qiurong is not a flat evil spirit; she is a woman whose identity has been slowly eaten away by the very act of staying alive.
guide.guide_3: Let’s walk through the moment of her death, because that’s where the real strangeness begins. Qiurong does not, in the moment she hits the water, become “the ghost from the well.” First, she drowns. That’s biology. Then her soul, still attached to the body by a thread of residual connection, floats upward a few inches and finds itself outside. She can see her own body being fished out. She can see her mother weeping. She tries to touch her mother’s sleeve and her hand goes through. At this point, she is not a dangerous spirit. She is a *Li Hun*—a freshly departed soul, no more threatening than a soap bubble. But the environment is lethal. The atmosphere of the living world is not designed for souls without a body. If she had left her body indoors, in a closed room, she might have lingered for a day or two. But she is in a well, and when morning comes, a single ray of sunlight hitting her ghostly hand will feel like someone poured hot oil on it. She retreats into the water, deep into the cold, and there she stays, because the water is the only barrier between her and annihilation. That is the first truth of Chinese ghost cosmology: death is not peace. It is exposure.
guide.guide_4: Here’s where the story gets philosophically nasty. The only way for a Li Hun to become strong enough to survive long-term is to consume other ghosts. Qiurong didn’t plan to. But after a few years, a wandering soul fell into her well—a peddler who had slipped and drowned. She felt his fear, his loneliness, and on pure instinct she pulled his essence into her own and absorbed it. Suddenly, she had a new set of memories: a stall in the market, a debt, a wife who nagged, the smell of fried dough in the morning. That’s not just information. That’s a whole person’s lifetime, stuffed into her brain alongside her own. She ate a maid a few years later, and now she also carried a girl’s love of embroidery and a bruise on her ribs from her master’s fist. Qiurong became a composite. Her original identity—the young woman who drowned herself in shame—was still there, but she was now surrounded by voices, memories, faces that were not hers. This is the *Li Gui* condition: a self that is not a self, a consciousness stitched together from others’ final thoughts. She wasn’t crazy. She was crowded.
guide.guide_5: Qiurong never tried to become a Ghost King or a Ghost Immortal. She could have, in theory—the path was there—but she wasn’t interested in power. She was interested in revenge. Every few years, a man would walk past the well, and she would call to him in a woman’s voice, soft and broken. He would lean over the edge, and she would rise, her face beautiful, her hair dripping, and she would pull him under. Each drowning was a small relief, a reenactment of the death that had defined her existence. But relief is not peace. It is a repetition compulsion. She drowned maybe a dozen men over three centuries. Each time, she felt the victim’s fear join the chorus inside her head. She never became a general of the dead; she remained a lonely predator in a single well. The Ghost King path and the Ghost Immortal path are two extreme fates in Chinese ghost mythology, but they are not the only fates. Most ghosts, like Qiurong, just stay where they are, too attached to one place and one memory to grow beyond it.
guide.guide_6: The Underworld finally caught her in the end. After a hundred years of being sealed by a Daoist talisman, she was freed, killed again, and then a Buddhist monk came. He sat by the well for three days, just reciting sutras. He did not try to exorcise her. He offered her an alternative to the endless loop of drowning. What he taught her was that her suffering was stored in the well’s memory, not in her own True Spirit—the part of her that was eternal and could not be contaminated. If she could let go of the well, she could let go of the pain. She agreed. The soul escorts came, and she went down to the Netherworld Court. At the Nie Jing Tai (Karma Mirror), she saw her whole life plainly, not as blame but as a record. Then she came to the River of Oblivion, where a woman whose name she would forget handed her a bowl. She drank. The well-water memory dissolved first, then her mother, then her own face. She became a clean soul and was reborn as a baby girl. The Underworld is not a hell in the Western sense; it is a processing center. Qiurong was not punished for the men she drowned—she was processed, cleaned, and sent back to try again.
guide.guide_7: What does Qiurong’s story ask us? It asks us to consider a radical idea about identity. In the Western intuition, you are your memories. Remove the memories, and you are not you. In the Chinese ghost cosmology, there is something underneath memory: the True Spirit (Zhen Ling), which is indestructible, unchangeable, and carries only the weight of karmic cause and effect, not personal history. Qiurong suffered for centuries as a composite of dozens of people. But when she drank the brew and forgot everything, the part of her that mattered—the part that could be set on a new path—remained untouched. This is not a comforting theology. It suggests that the “you” you think you are could be erased, and yet something essential would go on without you. Qiurong’s well, the water, the drowned men, the crying mother—all of it is gone, except in the story you just read. And the baby in a coastal town, now a young woman, will never know that she once drowned men to stay alive. That is the final weight of the Chinese ghost system: it is a machine that cares about the cycle, not about the person. Qiurong’s peace is real, but she paid for it with the complete destruction of her identity. Was it worth it? The story does not answer. It only offers the question.

lore_entries.description: A Li Gui (Vengeful Spirit) from Pu Songling’s *Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio*, a woman who drowned herself after being raped and haunted a well for centuries.
A ghost that has survived by consuming other wandering souls, accumulating their memories and obsessions into a composite self.
A Buddhist or Daoist ritual to guide a lingering soul away from its attachment to the mortal world and toward the cycle of reincarnation.
The River of Oblivion, the final boundary of the Underworld; those who cross it lose all memory and identity.
The old woman who administers the oblivion-brew to souls before they cross the River of Oblivion.
The Karma Mirror Platform before which a soul’s entire lifetime of actions is displayed without concealment.

faq_entries.question: What is Qiurong’s ghost type?
faq_entries.answer: She is a Li Gui (Vengeful Spirit), a ghost that has strengthened itself by consuming other wandering souls, leading to a composite and unstable identity.

faq_entries.question: Did Qiurong kill many people?
faq_entries.answer: Yes, she drowned at least a dozen men over three centuries by luring them to the well with her voice and beauty, then pulling them under.

faq_entries.question: How was Qiurong finally stopped?
faq_entries.answer: A high-level Buddhist monk performed a three-day chanting ritual and guided her to let go of her attachment to the well. She then accepted the Underworld’s summons and was reborn after drinking Meng Po’s brew.

faq_entries.question: Why did Qiurong become a ghost instead of going to the Underworld?
faq_entries.answer: Her intense anger and unresolved shame after the rape anchored her spirit to the well, preventing the natural gravitational pull of the Underworld from claiming her immediately.

faq_entries.question: What is the difference between Qiurong and a Western ghost?
faq_entries.answer: The Chinese ghost system is not about haunting for revenge in the afterlife; it is an intermediate state in a cycle of death, judgment, memory-wiping, and reincarnation. Qiurong’s identity was eroded by the souls she consumed, not by a single trauma alone.
